Task and constraints: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Builds all subsets by adding each input element to existing subsets or recursively choosing whether to include it.
Technique and why it applies: Subset generation fits because each element has two choices: absent or present.
Invariant: After processing a prefix, the result collection contains all subsets formed from that prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input should yield [[]]; duplicates in input can create duplicate value subsets unless deduplicated. The output is exponential.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*2^n) time and O(1) space, but output storage is O(n*2^n); recursive variants also use O(n) stack.

Task and constraints: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid. The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Starts a DFS from each board cell matching the first character, marks visited cells, and searches adjacent cells for the remaining word characters, restoring visited state after each branch.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking explores four-neighbor paths while a visited set prevents reusing a cell in one path.
Invariant: The current path matches a prefix of word and no cell on that path is reused.
Edge cases: A word longer than the number of cells cannot be found; one-character words succeed if present. Board mutation or visited bookkeeping must be undone after failed branches.
Complexity: No author time label was supplied. Worst-case search is exponential in word length per start cell; auxiliary path/visited space is O(L), excluding board and output.

Task and constraints: There is an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order (not necessarily with distinct values). The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Binary-searches a rotated sorted array with duplicates, discarding a half when sorted boundaries identify it; when boundary values are ambiguous, it shrinks an endpoint.
Technique and why it applies: Modified binary search uses sorted-half ordering, but duplicate values can make the pivot side ambiguous.
Invariant: The target, if still possible, remains inside the current low-to-high interval.
Edge cases: Repeated equal values may force one-step shrinking, degrading to linear time; empty input returns false if guarded by the code.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Average/best time is O(log n), worst case O(n) with duplicates; auxiliary space O(1).

Task and constraints: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar height where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram. The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Maintains a monotonic stack of bar indices and computes rectangle areas when a shorter bar closes a taller bar's span; a sentinel/cleanup handles remaining bars depending on variant.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic stack identifies each bar's maximal width before a lower bar blocks it.
Invariant: Stack heights remain monotonic, and popped bars are evaluated using the current index and new stack top as boundaries.
Edge cases: Equal heights follow the code's comparison rule; empty heights returns zero only if the implementation handles the empty stack. A final sentinel may be necessary.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space when supplied; each index is pushed and popped at most once, and stack storage can be O(n).

Task and constraints: Given a rows x cols binary matrix filled with 0's and 1's, find the largest rectangle containing only 1's and return its area. The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Treats each matrix row as the base of a histogram: consecutive ones increase column heights and zeros reset them, then the largest-rectangle routine evaluates the current heights.
Technique and why it applies: Histogram reduction converts a 2D all-ones rectangle into a 1D largest-rectangle problem per row.
Invariant: heights[j] equals the number of consecutive ones ending at the current row in column j.
Edge cases: An empty matrix returns zero when guarded; zero cells reset their columns. Each row's histogram is processed independently.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2) time and O(n) space; more precisely time is O(rows*cols) for a linear histogram scan per row and height/stack arrays use O(cols).

Task and constraints: We can scramble a string s to get a string t using the following algorithm: The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Checks whether two strings can be split at some position so their parts match either in the same order or swapped order, using recursive subproblems and memoization or substring tests as implemented.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive partitioning matches the definition of a scramble by testing split points and both child orderings.
Invariant: A memoized state represents whether the two selected substrings can be transformed into each other.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths fail immediately; identical strings may be a fast path. Slicing creates substrings and adds costs.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^4) time and O(n^3) space; these are bounds for memoized split-state DP, with substring allocation overhead depending on implementation.

Task and constraints: An n-bit gray code sequence is a sequence of 2^n integers where: The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Produces the Gray-code sequence by either applying i XOR (i shifted right one bit) for each integer or reflecting the previous sequence with a new leading bit.
Technique and why it applies: Bitwise Gray-code construction makes adjacent values differ in one bit.
Invariant: Each output is the Gray encoding of its index, or the reflected sequence preserves one-bit transitions.
Edge cases: n=0 returns [0]; sequence length is 2^n, so output itself grows exponentially.
Complexity: The author labels O(2^n) time; any returned list takes O(2^n) space, even if an auxiliary-space label says O(1).

Task and constraints: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicates, return all possible subsets (the power set). The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Sorts or incrementally extends subsets while avoiding duplicate combinations, typically skipping equal values at the same recursion level or removing duplicate candidate lists.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted subset enumeration can suppress duplicate subsets while considering each element's inclusion.
Invariant: Each generated subset uses input values, and equal-value branches are handled according to the variant's duplicate rule.
Edge cases: Repeated numbers require careful same-depth skipping; empty input returns the empty subset. Variants using candidate not in result incur expensive list comparisons.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*2^n) or a squared bound depending on variant; explicit duplicate-membership checks can add quadratic scans over generated subsets, so inspect the exact loop. Output storage remains O(n*2^n).

Task and constraints: A message containing letters from A-Z can be encoded into numbers using the following mapping: The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Uses dynamic programming to count decodings: a nonzero single digit contributes the previous count, and a valid two-digit number from 10 through 26 contributes the count two positions back.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix DP counts ways to decode a string by taking one or two digits at a time.
Invariant: The stored count represents the number of decodings of the prefix processed so far.
Edge cases: A leading zero or invalid zero pair returns zero; empty input handling depends on the implementation. Two-digit checks must exclude values above 26.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space when supplied; rolling counts use constant auxiliary storage, while memoized variants use O(n).

Task and constraints: A valid IP address consists of exactly four integers separated by single dots. Each integer is between 0 and 255 (inclusive) and cannot have leading zeros. The method follows the input and output described in the statement.
Idea: Tries every split of the digit string into four parts, accepts segments with values 0..255 and no illegal leading zeros, and joins valid groups with dots.
Technique and why it applies: Bounded backtracking fits because an IPv4 address has exactly four decimal segments, each at most three digits.
Invariant: The partial result contains valid segments from the consumed prefix, and remaining characters must still fit into remaining segments.
Edge cases: Segments like '0' are valid but '00' is rejected; lengths outside 4..12 cannot form four valid segments. Integer conversion is applied to short segments only.
Complexity: The author labels O(3^4) search and O(n*m) space; the search has at most three candidate segment lengths per each of four positions, plus output storage.
